_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-06) review fixes: explain.steps[2], the sequence diagram, its aria and caption, the TLS handshake and Session keys terms and the interview answer now follow TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446): the two hellos carry key shares, so everything after them is encrypted, then the certificate and proof arrive encrypted, then the browser's checks, then Finished, then the request; new terms Key share, Finished and TLS 1.3; option D part2, the fix and the r4 model no longer say renew every 60 days, which source 2 says will stop being enough once certificates last 64 days (February 2027): they say renew at two thirds of the lifetime or when ARI says, and part2 defines ARI where it is first used; realWorld[2] quotes that warning; option B part2 now has the 30-day alarm in late March (a 200-day certificate from 6 October 2026 expires about 24 April 2027); realWorld[0] says the status posts, not Microsoft, didn't say which certificate; the Padlock term notes Chrome's tune icon since Chrome 117 (September 2023), with the Chromium blog added to sources; the sim's manual renewal now follows the date's limit (100 days from 15 March 2027)
title: The Padlock

post.author: u/overnight_rx_mina
post.title: I fill online prescription orders overnight. At midnight our website stopped being us.

blocks.text: I'm the overnight technician at Larkspur Pharmacy, the 24-hour one across from the hospital. Online refill orders print behind the counter all night, and I fill them for morning pickup. A normal night is forty to sixty orders.
Last night the printer went quiet at 11:58 PM. At 12:20 AM the phone rang.
"Your website says you're pretending to be yourselves," said Mrs. Okafor. She has ordered her husband's heart pills from us every month for six years.

I opened larkspurrx.com on the counter computer. A full red page: *Your connection is not private. Attackers might be trying to steal your information.* The little padlock next to our address, the one that means nobody in between can read what you send, was gone. Same on my phone. Same on the hospital Wi-Fi. Not one customer. Everyone.
Our refill app didn't show a warning at all. It just said *Something went wrong* and kept spinning.
I clicked the warning for details. It showed our certificate, the digital ID card a website hands your browser to prove who it is:

subject     larkspurrx.com
issued by   Northgate Trust CA
valid from  Mon 6 Oct 2025, 00:00
expires     Tue 6 Oct 2026, 00:00
error       NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID
Our name. The same signer. Nothing about us had changed except the date.
At 3 AM I found an index card taped inside the server cupboard, in the handwriting of Dev, who built our site and left in April.

Nobody has opened Dev's mailbox since he left. The password was on the back of the card. Four unread emails from Northgate, one subject line: *Your certificate for larkspurrx.com expires in 30 days.* Then 14. Then 7. Then 1.
Somebody had been warning us for a month. Every warning went to a man who doesn't work here anymore.

Thirty-one people called before 6 AM. One man said he clicked *proceed anyway* and typed in his card number. The owner will buy a new certificate when the office opens. Then what? Set an alarm for next October? And why does the browser call us attackers, when the only thing that changed was the calendar?

blocks.label: certificate_check.png

diagram.aria: What the browser checked at 12:20 AM on Tuesday 6 October. On the left, the certificate chain: Northgate Root, which is in the browser's list of trusted roots, signed Northgate Trust CA, which signed the certificate for larkspurrx.com, issued 6 October 2025 and expiring 6 October 2026 at 00:00. On the right, the browser's three checks: the signer is trusted, yes. The name matches, yes. Still in date, no, it expired 20 minutes ago.

blocks.caption: I drew what the browser checked at 12:20 AM. The chain still leads to a root it trusts, and the name still matches. Only the date fails, and one failed check is enough for the red page.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Read your log again. Who it's for: still you. Who signed it: still them. The only line that changed has a date on it. A padlock is a promise with an end date, and someone built it that way on purpose. Ask why.

replies.author: u/overnight_rx_mina
replies.text: So a fake one can't stay good forever? I'm a pharmacy tech. Until tonight I thought the padlock just came with the website.

comments.author: u/rack_rat_wendell
comments.text: Quick glossary, since nobody gave you one. HTTPS is the web's normal language, HTTP, sent through an encrypted tunnel called TLS. Your certificate proves the tunnel really leads to larkspurrx.com. It's signed by a certificate authority (CA), a company browsers trust to check that you really control the name. Northgate is one. There are free ones too, like Let's Encrypt, where a small program on your server renews the certificate by itself every couple of months using a standard called ACME. No index cards.

comments.author: u/night_nurse_pell
comments.text: Mine went red at 11:46 PM. Fourteen minutes before yours. My laptop clock runs fourteen minutes fast, on purpose, so I'm never late for shift.

comments.author: u/third_party_tom
comments.text: Tell the man who clicked *proceed anyway* to call his bank tonight. Your site was probably fine. But that button is exactly what someone pretending to be you would want him to press.

reply.prompt: The owner wants to make sure the padlock never breaks again. What should she do? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Buy the longest certificate money can buy, five or ten years if possible, so this only happens once a decade.
options.part2: The owner called three certificate companies. All three said the same thing: no public certificate can last longer than 200 days now, and the limit keeps shrinking. She bought a 200-day one and wrote the new date on Dev's index card. In April the printer went quiet at midnight again. This time I knew what the red page meant. Knowing didn't make it go away.
options.senior: Browsers and certificate authorities shortened lifetimes on purpose: 200 days since March 2026, 100 days from March 2027, 47 days from March 2029. Long certificates are gone. The only lasting fix is to stop renewing by hand.

options.text: Keep renewing by hand, but send the reminder emails to a shared pharmacy inbox and put three alarms in the shop calendar: 30, 14 and 7 days before expiry.
options.part2: We pointed the reminders at the shared inbox and set the alarms. In late March the 30-day alarm went off. The owner was on holiday, the relief pharmacist thought I handled it, and I thought the owner did. On day 7 I called Northgate myself, paid with my own card, and spent two hours on hold learning how to install it. The padlock held. Barely.
options.senior: A shared inbox beats one person's mailbox, but it still depends on a human acting, twice a year now and more often every year as lifetimes shrink. Reminders tell you about a problem. They don't fix it.

options.text: Post a notice telling customers the warning is harmless and they can safely click *proceed anyway* until it's fixed.
options.verdict: Teaches customers to ignore the alarm
options.part2: The owner posted the notice on our page and people clicked through. Two weeks later, long after the new certificate was in, a man on the hospital café Wi-Fi got the same red page on our site. He remembered the notice and clicked through. This time it wasn't an expired certificate. Someone on that Wi-Fi was pretending to be us.
options.senior: The browser can't tell an expired certificate from an impostor's, so it shows the same alarm for both. Teaching people to click past it trains them to ignore the one warning that protects them from a real attack.

options.text: Switch to automatic renewal with ACME (Let's Encrypt, or the hosting company's built-in certificates), and add a separate check that alerts a shared team inbox if the live site's certificate has fewer than 20 days left.
options.part2: Wendell from the comments set it up on Saturday. A small program on our server now renews the certificate by itself once two thirds of its life has passed, or sooner if the certificate authority's ARI says so. ARI, short for ACME Renewal Information, is a note the CA publishes for each certificate saying when it should be renewed. A monitoring service checks the live site every night and emails the pharmacy's shared inbox if fewer than 20 days are left. Nobody has touched it since. Last night the monitor emailed anyway. Not about larkspurrx.com. About old-orders.larkspurrx.com, 12 days left. None of us knew it existed. Dev's again. Still running somewhere, still answering, still counting down.
options.senior: Automate the renewal, then watch the result separately, because automation fails quietly. Check the certificate the live site actually serves, not just the renewal job, keep a list of every certificate you own, and send alerts to a team, never to one person.

sim.title: Watch the padlock checks
sim.lede: You're the pharmacy. Each dot is one customer connecting to larkspurrx.com: a browser, with a person looking at it, or the refill app, a program with no page to show. The clock runs 60 times faster than real life and starts 15 minutes before the certificate expires. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Watch the date check fail at midnight. Browsers show the red page, the app just fails. Renew by hand and see how many days you bought. Then reset, turn on auto-renew and skip ahead 30 days at a time. Finally, with auto-renew still on, install the certificate for the wrong name and see what automation can't fix.

explain.oneLine: Nobody attacked Larkspur. Its certificate, the digital identity card that proves the site is really larkspurrx.com, reached its expiry date at midnight, and browsers refuse a certificate they can no longer trust.

steps.title: HTTPS is HTTP inside a locked tunnel.
steps.text: Plain HTTP travels like a postcard: anyone along the way, such as whoever runs a café's Wi-Fi, can read it or change it. HTTPS sends the same HTTP through TLS, a layer that gives three things. Privacy: the data is encrypted, scrambled so only the two ends can read it. Integrity: any change on the way is detected. Identity: the browser can tell it is really talking to larkspurrx.com. The padlock means all three are in place.

steps.title: Identity comes from a certificate and a chain of signatures.
steps.text: A certificate is a small file that says: this public key belongs to larkspurrx.com, from this date until that date. A certificate authority (CA) signs it after checking that Larkspur controls the name. Browsers and operating systems ship with a short list of root certificates they trust. A root signs an intermediate, the intermediate signs the site's certificate, and the browser follows those signatures up to a root it already knows. That trail of signatures is the chain of trust.

steps.title: The TLS handshake checks the certificate before the request goes out.
steps.text: Right after the TCP handshake comes the TLS handshake. In TLS 1.3, the browser's hello lists what it supports and carries a key share, its half of a key exchange. The server's hello carries the server's half. From those two halves both sides work out the same fresh session keys, so everything after the hellos is encrypted. Then the server sends its certificate chain, already encrypted, proves it holds the matching private key by signing the handshake, and sends Finished, a seal over the whole exchange. The browser runs three checks: does the chain end at a trusted root, does the name match the address, and is the time now between the certificate's two dates? If all pass, the browser sends its own Finished and the HTTP request goes through encrypted. If any check fails, a browser shows a warning page and an app simply gives up.

steps.title: At 00:00 the date check started failing for everyone.
steps.text: Larkspur's certificate was valid from 6 October 2025 until 6 October 2026 at 00:00. Nothing about the server changed at midnight. Every browser compared that end date with its own clock and refused. A browser can't tell an expired certificate from a forged one, so it shows the same alarm it shows for an impostor. The night nurse saw it 14 minutes early because her laptop's clock runs 14 minutes fast.

steps.title: Expiry is a feature, and lifetimes keep shrinking.
steps.text: If a private key leaks, or a certificate is issued by mistake, a short life limits how long it can be abused. So the rules keep cutting lifetimes: public certificates could last 398 days until March 2026, now 200, from March 2027 100 days, and from March 2029 just 47. At that pace, renewing by hand stops being a chore and becomes a guaranteed outage. That is why ACME exists.

diagram.aria: The TLS 1.3 handshake between a browser and the pharmacy server. After the TCP handshake, the browser and the server each send a hello carrying a key share, and from the two shares both sides make the same session keys, so everything after the hellos is encrypted. The server sends its certificate chain, then proof that it holds the private key and its Finished message. The browser checks chain, name and date, sends its own Finished, and only then do the encrypted request and response flow. Outcome: from 00:00 on 6 October the date check fails and the browser shows a red warning page.

steps.text: From 00:00: date check fails, red page

explain.caption: Read top to bottom. The TCP handshake from case 3 comes first. Then TLS 1.3: two hellos carrying key shares, after which everything is encrypted, the certificate included. The server proves it holds the private key, the browser runs its three checks and sends Finished, and only then does the request go. From 00:00 on Tuesday the third check, the date, failed, so every customer's conversation stopped at the checks.

fix.title: The fix: automate renewal, then watch it separately
fix.text: Use ACME, the standard protocol certificate authorities use to issue certificates with no human involved. A small ACME client on the server (or your hosting or cloud provider's built-in certificates) proves to the CA that you control the name, usually by publishing a file or a DNS record the CA asks for, then fetches the new certificate and reloads the server. Let's Encrypt, a free CA, issues 90-day certificates today and will cut that to 64 days in February 2027 and 45 days in February 2028, so don't renew on a fixed timer such as every 60 days. Renew once about two thirds of the certificate's lifetime has passed, or when ARI, the CA's own renewal hint for each certificate, says to. Then add an independent monitor that checks the certificate the live site actually serves and alerts a shared team channel when fewer than, say, 20 days remain. Keep a list of every certificate you own, old subdomains included, with an owner for each.

limits: Automation fails quietly. A firewall change, a DNS change or a server that never reloads the new file can stop renewals with nobody noticing. That is why the separate monitor matters, and why Let's Encrypt, which stopped sending expiry reminder emails in June 2025, tells people to monitor instead.

A padlock proves the name, not the business. A CA checks that you control larkspurrx.com, not that you're an honest pharmacy, so a scam site with a look-alike name can have a perfect padlock. And TLS protects data only on the way: it does nothing for a hacked server or the data stored on it.

Some trust is out of your hands. Old devices carry old lists of trusted roots, and a wrong clock on a customer's laptop breaks the date check from their side, as the night nurse saw. When a root itself expires, devices that never got the newer root show warnings on sites that did nothing wrong.

head: How you renew
Good
Bad
rows: 200 days now and falling. Someone must remember, and people leave.
ACME client on your own server
You run and update the client, and it can fail silently, so you still need a monitor.
Managed by your cloud or host
Renews itself for the services they run, such as AWS load balancers.
Covers only what they host. Certificates you import or copy elsewhere are still yours to renew.

explain.seniorTake: Certificates don't fail. Calendars do. Treat every certificate as a timer that is already running: let one machine renew it, let a different machine watch the live site, and send the alarm to a team, never to one person's inbox.

realWorld.title: Microsoft Teams, February 3, 2020
realWorld.text: TechCrunch reported Teams, Microsoft's workplace chat and meetings app, down from about 8:30 AM US Eastern time on a Monday. Around 10 AM, Microsoft's status account posted that it had "determined that an authentication certificate has expired causing users to have issues using the service" and that it was developing a fix to apply a new certificate. It then began deploying the updated certificate. The status posts didn't say which certificate it was or why it lapsed. One expired certificate was enough to lock users out.

realWorld.title: Let's Encrypt: short on purpose
realWorld.text: Let's Encrypt, a free certificate authority, has issued 90-day certificates from the start. In 2015 it gave two reasons: short lifetimes limit the damage from stolen keys and from certificates issued by mistake, and they encourage automation, which it called absolutely essential.

realWorld.title: Let's Encrypt: 45 days by 2028
realWorld.text: In December 2025 Let's Encrypt announced it will move its default certificates to 64 days in February 2027 and 45 days in February 2028. Its advice: let your ACME client renew automatically, at about two thirds of the certificate's lifetime if it can't use ACME Renewal Information, don't renew by hand, and monitor so you hear when a renewal fails. It warns that renewing at a hardcoded interval of 60 days will no longer be sufficient.

realWorld.title: The industry's schedule
realWorld.text: In April 2025 the CA/Browser Forum, the group of certificate authorities and browser makers that writes the rules every public certificate follows, voted to shrink the longest a certificate may last. The Baseline Requirements now set 200 days for certificates issued from March 15, 2026, 100 days from March 15, 2027, and 47 days from March 15, 2029. Before that the limit was 398 days, which is how Larkspur's October 2025 certificate could last a full year.

realWorld.title: When a root expires: September 30, 2021
realWorld.text: Trust has dates at the top of the chain too. For years, Let's Encrypt certificates were also vouched for by an older root, DST Root CA X3, through a cross-sign, so devices that didn't yet know Let's Encrypt's own root, ISRG Root X1, still trusted them. When that cross-sign expired on September 30, 2021, older devices that didn't trust ISRG Root X1 started getting certificate warnings on sites that had done nothing wrong.

asked: What happens when you visit an https:// website?
A certificate expired and took production down. How do you make sure it never happens again?
interview.answer: Walk the layers: DNS gives the IP address, TCP connects, then the TLS handshake. In TLS 1.3 the two hellos carry key shares, so both sides have session keys after one round trip and everything after is encrypted. The server's certificate chain and its proof of the private key arrive encrypted, the client checks the chain up to a trusted root, the hostname and the validity dates, both sides send Finished, and HTTP runs encrypted inside. For the outage: automate issuance and renewal with ACME or a managed service such as AWS Certificate Manager, renew at about two thirds of the lifetime or when ARI says, never on a fixed timer, monitor the certificate each live endpoint actually serves with alerts well before expiry going to a team, and keep an inventory of every certificate with an owner. Name the limits before they ask: automation can fail silently, lifetimes are shrinking to 47 days by 2029, and client clocks and trust stores are outside your control.

terms.def: The lock icon next to a web address: the TLS checks passed, so the connection is encrypted and the site proved its name. Chrome shows a "tune" icon there instead since version 117 (September 2023).
HTTP sent through TLS. The same requests and responses as HTTP, but encrypted, protected from changes, and with the site's identity checked. Addresses start with https://.
Transport Layer Security: the layer that encrypts a connection, detects tampering and proves the server's identity. HTTPS is HTTP running inside TLS.
Secure Sockets Layer, the older protocol TLS replaced. People still say "SSL certificate" when they mean a TLS certificate.
Scrambling data with a key so that only someone holding the right key can read it.
What TLS's encryption gives you: people between you and the site, like whoever runs a café's Wi-Fi, can see that you connected but not what you sent or received.
Knowing data wasn't changed on the way. TLS detects any change in transit and drops the connection.
Proof that you're talking to the real owner of the name. In TLS the server shows its certificate and proves it holds the matching private key.
A small signed file, a website's ID card. It names the site, holds its public key, and says from when until when it's valid. A certificate authority signs it.
CA for short. An organisation browsers trust to check that whoever asks for a certificate really controls the name, and then to sign it. Let's Encrypt is a free one.
The half of a key pair that can be shared with anyone. Signatures made with the private key can be checked with it.
The secret half of a key pair. The server keeps it and uses it to prove it owns its certificate. If it leaks, anyone holding it can pretend to be the site.
A stamp made with a private key that anyone can check with the matching public key. It proves who signed and that nothing changed since.
A CA's top-level certificate, built into browsers and operating systems. It's trusted without anyone vouching for it, and its key is kept offline.
A certificate signed by a root, which a CA uses day to day to sign websites' certificates, so the root's key can stay locked away.
The path of signatures from a site's certificate, through an intermediate, up to a root the browser already trusts. If a link is missing or wrong, the check fails.
The list of root certificates a browser or operating system trusts. Old devices have old lists.
The name in the address, like larkspurrx.com. The certificate must cover that exact name, or the browser refuses it.
A name under your domain, like old-orders.larkspurrx.com. Each one needs a certificate that covers it, and each one can expire on its own.
The "not after" date in a certificate. From that moment on, browsers and apps treat it as invalid, even if nothing else changed.

The short exchange at the start of a TLS connection: two hellos that set up session keys, then the server's certificate and proof, the client's checks, and Finished. It comes right after the TCP handshake.
The current version of TLS, defined in RFC 8446 (2018). Its handshake takes one round trip, and everything after the two hellos is encrypted.
In TLS 1.3, each side's half of a key exchange, sent in its hello. From the two halves both sides compute the same session keys, and the keys themselves never cross the network.
Fresh, temporary keys both sides work out from the two key shares in the hellos, and use to encrypt the rest of that one conversation.
The last TLS handshake message from each side: a seal over the whole handshake that proves both sides saw the same messages and hold the same keys.
The full-page alarm a browser shows when a TLS check fails, such as "Your connection is not private." You can click past it, and almost never should.
A certificate signed by its own key instead of a CA. No chain leads to a trusted root, so browsers reject it.
What a CA does when it creates and signs a certificate for someone. The site owner then installs it on their server.
Getting a new certificate for the same name before the old one expires, and installing it on the server.
The HTTP method for reading, as in GET /refills: "send me the refills page". It asks for something without changing it.
What the server sends back to a request: a status code such as 200 OK, headers, and usually a body, like the page itself.
The status code for a request that worked.
One address that clients connect to, such as larkspurrx.com or api.larkspurrx.com. Each one presents its own certificate.
Automatic Certificate Management Environment: the standard protocol (RFC 8555) a server uses to prove it controls a name and get or renew a certificate with no human involved.
The small program on a server that speaks ACME: on a schedule it proves control of the name, fetches the new certificate and installs it.
ARI for short. A way for a CA to tell ACME clients when to renew each certificate, so renewals happen at the right moment, or early if the CA needs them to.
A free, non-profit certificate authority that issues certificates only through ACME. Its default certificates last 90 days in 2026, falling to 45 days by 2028.
How a CA checks you control a name: it asks you to publish a specific file on the site or a specific DNS record, then looks for it.
Checking a system automatically and often, and raising an alert when something looks wrong, such as a certificate with fewer than 20 days left.
A filter that decides which network traffic may pass. A new firewall rule can block the CA's validation check and quietly stop renewals.
When a private key leaks or is stolen. Whoever has it can impersonate the site until the certificate expires or is revoked.
To cancel a certificate before its expiry date, for example after its private key leaks.
Here, a server pretending to be a site it isn't, such as an attacker on shared Wi-Fi answering in the real site's place. TLS's checks are what stop it.
The group of certificate authorities and browser makers that sets the rules all public certificates follow, including how long they may last.
The CA/Browser Forum's rulebook for public TLS certificates. It sets, among other things, the longest a certificate may be valid.
When one CA's root signs another CA's certificate, so devices that trust the first also trust the second. New CAs use it until their own root is widely known.
Microsoft's chat and video meetings app for workplaces.
A certificate a service uses to prove its identity, for example when signing users in or when its own parts talk to each other. When it expires, those checks fail.
A server that receives incoming traffic and spreads it across several servers behind it. On AWS it often holds the site's certificate.
Amazon's content delivery network: servers around the world that keep copies of your site near users and serve it over HTTPS with your certificate.
One of AWS's geographic areas, a group of data centers in one part of the world. Many services, ACM certificates included, live separately in each Region.
ACM for short. Amazon's certificate service. It issues free public certificates for AWS services and renews them itself; certificates you import, you renew yourself.
Amazon's monitoring service. It stores metrics, such as a certificate's days to expiry, and can raise alarms when they cross a line.
Amazon's event service. It delivers events, such as "certificate approaching expiration", to whatever you connect, like an email or a ticket.

atWork: In the AWS console, open AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) in each Region your team uses and sort the certificates by expiry date. For each one, check whether ACM issued it (with DNS validation, ACM renews those itself while they're in use with a service such as a load balancer or CloudFront) or whether it was imported (ACM never renews those; a person or a script must). Then look for a CloudWatch alarm on the DaysToExpiry metric, or an EventBridge rule on the "ACM Certificate Approaching Expiration" event, that alerts a team rather than one person. Finally, list the certificates that live outside AWS, such as on old servers and subdomains, and give each one an owner.

recall.prompt: Your company's main website certificate expires in 9 days. It has been renewed by hand once a year, and the person who did it last year has left. What do you do this week, and what do you change for good?

keyIdeas.idea: Renew it now, before it expires, and check the live site serves the new one
Automate renewal with ACME or a managed service
Monitor the live certificate's expiry and alert a team, not one person

recall.model: This week: renew it by hand, install it, and check that the live site actually serves the new certificate. For good: move it to automatic renewal, with an ACME client on the server or a managed service such as AWS Certificate Manager, renewing at about two thirds of its lifetime. Add a separate monitor that checks the certificate the live site serves and alerts a team channel when fewer than about 20 days remain, and keep a list of every certificate with an owner. Lifetimes are shrinking to 47 days by 2029, so renewing by hand won't survive anyway.

recall.prompt: At midnight every browser showed Larkspur's red warning page, though nothing on the server had changed. Which check failed?
options: The chain: the signer was no longer trusted
The name: the certificate was for a different site
The date: the certificate's expiry had passed
The server stopped answering on its port
recall.why: The chain and the name still checked out. The certificate's end date was 6 October 2026 at 00:00, and every browser compared it with its own clock.

recall.prompt: How does a browser decide whether to trust larkspurrx.com's certificate?
options: It looks up the site's IP address through DNS
It follows signatures from the site's certificate up through an intermediate to a root already in its trust store
It asks the site for a password
It checks how many years the site has existed
recall.why: That path of signatures is the chain of trust. The browser only trusts roots it already ships with, and each certificate below must be signed by the one above.

recall.prompt: A teammate says: "Our certificate renews itself with an ACME client, so we don't need any monitoring." What could still go wrong, and what do you suggest?

keyIdeas.idea: Monitor the certificate the live site actually serves
Alert a team well before expiry

recall.model: Automation fails quietly: a firewall or DNS change can block the CA's validation, the client can crash or stop being scheduled, or the server can keep serving the old file because it never reloaded. Keep the ACME client, and add an independent monitor that connects to the live site, reads the certificate it actually serves and alerts a team when fewer than about 20 days remain. With a 90-day certificate renewed once two thirds of its life has passed, about 30 days before expiry, an alert at 20 days left means renewal has been failing for 10 days, with time left to fix it. Renew by that fraction or when ARI says, never on a fixed 60-day timer, because lifetimes are shrinking to 64 days in 2027 and 45 in 2028, and keep the alert line below the renewal point as they shrink.

recall.prompt: Which of these does TLS NOT protect you from?
options: Someone on café Wi-Fi reading the password you send
A device along the way changing the page you receive
A scam site with a look-alike name and its own valid certificate
A server pretending to be the real larkspurrx.com
recall.why: A CA only checks that the scam site controls its own look-alike name, so its padlock is genuine. TLS proves you reached the name in the address bar, not that the name belongs to an honest business.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The website's certificate has renewed itself twice. Then last night at 2 AM the refill app stopped working, while the site loaded fine in every browser. It turns out the app talks to api.larkspurrx.com, a separate server Dev set up, with its own certificate, renewed by hand. It was on nobody's list. The owner asks how we keep finding these.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What happened, and how do you stop the next one?

keyIdeas.idea: The app's server had its own certificate, and it expired
Apps fail without a warning page, so it looks mysterious
Keep an inventory of every certificate and monitor each endpoint

coldCase.model: The website and the API are different servers with different certificates. The API's certificate, renewed by hand and on nobody's list, expired at 2 AM. A browser would have shown a red page, but the app is a program: its TLS check failed and it just errored, which is why it looked like a mystery. Put the API on the same automatic renewal, then build an inventory of every name and server that presents a certificate, old ones included, and point the expiry monitor at all of them, alerting a team. Better still, regularly list every name in your DNS so new ones can't hide.

next: Next: a night guard counts the doors in Room 3 every night. The kiosk keeps counting more.
